### BLOCKER 1 — pod_id-pinning may make the predicate NEVER fire: the infra-respawn re-provisions a FRESH pod (new pod_id), so crash #2 lands on a different pod_id and is counted as a "first crash"

**Grounding.** Plan §2 row 3 + §4 "Trust-the-respawn-happened": the predicate
assumes "the orphan-reap respawn runs on the SAME host pod-A" so that a second
same-signature CUDA-IMA on the SAME pod_id is the wedge signal. The pod_id
pinning is load-bearing — §2 conjunct 2 ("the prior-crash record is keyed to
`_runpod_handle_identity` … the OLD record doesn't match the fresh pod") and §6
("1st→record{pod-A}; 2nd→escalate").

But the autonomous respawn path does NOT guarantee same-pod. A CUDA-IMA /
`EngineDeadError` crash classifies `failure_class: infra` (verified:
`scripts/failure_classifier.py:93-96` — `Traceback.*\b(vllm|…)/ ` matches any
vLLM-framed traceback → `infra`; not `code`). And `/issue` Step 7's infra route
is, verbatim, `.claude/agents/experimenter.md:197-199`:

> "`/issue` Step 7 routes `failure_class: infra` back to a fresh experimenter
> respawn (cap 3) **after the lifecycle layer terminates + re-provisions a clean
> pod**."

A terminate + re-provision writes a NEW `pod_name` to the sidecar. So the
sequence the plan needs ("crash on pod-A → respawn on pod-A → crash again on
pod-A") is in tension with the actual autonomous recovery ("crash on pod-A →
terminate pod-A + re-provision pod-B → crash on pod-B"). Under the pod_id-pinned
record, the pod-B crash reads as a FIRST crash (no prior record for pod-B) — the
escalation never fires, the run burns all 3 infra respawns on fresh pods, each
re-crashing identically, and finally exhausts the cap WITHOUT ever taking the
CUDA-IMA failover the plan exists to provide. This is exactly the "pod_id
resetting between crashes due to a watcher-side stop/resume" edge case.

This is conclusion-changing: the fix as specified can be inert on the very path
(#763 was an autonomous run) it was written to handle. The plan's own §4
"Invalidated if a respawn path ever skips the reap" guard is aimed at the wrong
failure — the problem isn't a SKIPPED reap, it's a respawn on a DIFFERENT pod.

**Fix (pick one, state it in §4):**
(a) Resolve definitively whether the experimenter infra-respawn for a vLLM-engine
crash is same-pod (in-place SSH relaunch — `experimenter.md` Pre-Launch step 9,
GCP-lane salvage-relaunch §) or fresh-pod (terminate + re-provision — line 198),
and if it can be EITHER, key the repeat-count on something that survives a
fresh-pod re-provision but still localizes to one PHYSICAL host (the
re-provision can land on a new RunPod host OR the same one). pod_name does not
do this. If the autonomous path is reliably fresh-pod, the "same pod_id"
predicate is the wrong signal entirely and the design needs to count
same-signature CUDA-IMA repeats across the RUN (bounded, with the orphan-reap as
the between-crash event), not per pod_id.
(b) If you keep pod_id-pinning, the plan must DEMONSTRATE (not assert) that the
infra-respawn for this crash class is in-place same-pod — cite the exact Step 7
branch + experimenter step that relaunches on the SAME pod for a vLLM
`EngineDeadError`, and add an integration test that exercises the
crash→respawn-same-pod→crash sequence end to end, not just two scripted polls
with a hand-set identical pod_name.

mechanizable: yes — a test asserting the full classify→respawn→re-poll loop
preserves (or does not preserve) pod_name across an infra-respawn would catch
this; the unit tests in §3d all hand-construct an identical pod_name and so
cannot.

### BLOCKER 2 — the signature regex keys on `result.log_tail_excerpt`, which is ONLY the last 5 log lines; the CUDA-IMA / EngineDeadError signature usually is NOT in those 5 lines

**Grounding.** Plan §2 conjunct 1 + §3 (`CUDA_IMA_SIGNATURE.search(result.log_tail_excerpt)`)
+ Assumption "`PollResult.log_tail_excerpt` carries the crash signature (HIGH; read
code)". But `log_tail_excerpt` is constructed at
`scripts/poll_pipeline.py:2695-2698`:

```python
if cell_mtime_epoch > 0 and cell_mtime_epoch > mtime_epoch:
    tail_excerpt = "\n".join(probe["cell_log_tail"].splitlines()[-5:])
else:
    tail_excerpt = "\n".join(probe["log_tail"].splitlines()[-5:])
```

It is the LAST 5 LINES only. A vLLM CUDA-IMA death is a long traceback; the
signature lines (`CUDA error: an illegal memory access was encountered`,
`EngineDeadError`, `EngineCore … died`) are routinely NOT in the final 5 lines —
the tail is frequently the Python process exit, a `subprocess` returncode line,
the `ZeroDivisionError` tqdm artifact (gotchas.md #628/#613), or a generic
re-raise. The plan's "HIGH confidence; read code" rests on the signature TEXT
existing somewhere in the cell log, but the predicate only sees 5 lines of it.
The probability the IMA signature lands in exactly those 5 lines is not
characterized — and where it doesn't, the predicate silently never matches, the
record is never written, and the failover never fires.

Note this is the same `log_tail_excerpt` that `failure_classifier` does NOT use
for the infra-vs-code call (the classifier reads the full `epm:failure` body via
`classify_failure(body)`), so "the crash classified infra" does NOT imply "the
5-line excerpt carries the IMA signature." The two consumers read different
surfaces.

**Fix (pick one, name it in §4 + add a test):**
(a) Match the regex against the SAME full-body surface the failure-classifier
sees (the `epm:failure` body / full `probe["log_tail"]` / `cell_log_tail`), not
the 5-line `log_tail_excerpt`. This requires the escalation to read a wider
surface than `result.log_tail_excerpt` — a real design change, not a string
tweak.
(b) Widen `log_tail_excerpt` (or add a dedicated wider field) so the IMA
signature is reliably present — but that touches `poll_pipeline.py`'s
notification surface and risks other consumers.
(c) Demonstrate empirically against the #763 cell log that the IMA signature IS
in the last 5 lines for THIS workload class, and scope the predicate to that —
but #763's actual log lines are not in the plan, and the implementer "adjusts
the regex" deviation (§12) cannot fix a truncation problem by re-wording the
regex.

mechanizable: yes — a test feeding a realistic multi-line vLLM IMA traceback
through the real `poll_once` excerpt construction (last-5-lines) and asserting
`CUDA_IMA_SIGNATURE.search(excerpt)` would catch the truncation; the §3d tests
as listed inject a `log_tail_excerpt` that already contains the signature, so
they assume away the bug.

### MAJOR 1 — §3a's function table omits the terminal-CODE emit helper that §6 requires; `_terminal_infra_json` hardcodes `failure_class: infra`

**Grounding.** §6 routes the once-more-bound exhaustion to "TERMINAL
failure_class: code (`runpod_cuda_ima_failover_exhausted`) → blocked" and the
narrative says "the existing `_terminal_infra_json` + a new terminal-code emit."
But `scripts/backend_poll.py:1452` hardcodes `"failure_class": "infra"` in
`_terminal_infra_json`, and the §3a function table (lines 70-82) lists NO
`_terminal_code_json` helper. The watcher's capacity-retry gate keys exactly on
this: `autonomous_session_watch.py:8458` — `retriable = failure_class == "infra"
and reason in TRANSIENT_CAPACITY_REASONS`. So if the exhaustion path emitted a
`failure_class: infra` JSON (the only emit helper §3a enumerates), AND the reason
happened to be mis-set, the run could be wrongly re-driven; conversely an
`infra`+non-transient reason parks at blocked but mislabels the failure class.
The bound's CORRECTNESS (park at blocked, never re-drive) depends on emitting a
genuine `failure_class: code` JSON, which needs a helper the plan doesn't list.

**Fix:** add `_terminal_code_json` (or a `failure_class` kwarg to
`_terminal_infra_json` — but that function's name + docstring assert infra, so a
sibling is cleaner) to §3a and an acceptance criterion that the exhaustion JSON
carries `failure_class: code`. Confirm against `autonomous_session_watch.py:8458`
that the watcher then parks it at blocked. This is a real gap but recoverable in
the revise round (it's an enumeration omission, not a design flaw).

mechanizable: yes — `test_poller_cuda_ima_failover_exhausted_emits_code` (already
in §3d) should assert `out["failure_class"] == "code"`, AND a test asserting the
watcher's `_is_transient_capacity_block` returns False on that JSON closes the
loop.

### MAJOR 2 — the new `result = _maybe_escalate_runpod_cuda_ima(...)` runs AFTER `_maybe_escalate_runpod_wedge`, which can rewrite `status=dead → status=running` within the no-port K window; verify the ordering does not mask a CUDA-IMA dead poll

**Grounding.** The plan's `main()` wiring (§3a lines 86-99) inserts the CUDA-IMA
block AFTER the Part C no-port block (`backend_poll.py:1850-1881`).
`_maybe_escalate_runpod_wedge` (lines 666-701) rewrites an SSH-dead poll to
`status="running"` when the pod is RUNNING-but-no-port WITHIN K. If a CUDA-IMA
crash leaves the pod momentarily no-port (engine dead, ports not yet torn down),
the no-port escalation would flip `status=dead → running` BEFORE the CUDA-IMA
predicate runs — and `_is_runpod_cuda_ima_failure` requires `status=="dead"`
(§3a). The CUDA-IMA crash would then be absorbed into the no-port-clock path and
never recorded as a CUDA-IMA crash. In the common case the CUDA-IMA pod keeps its
port + stays RUNNING (plan §1 motivating-incident: "keeps its port + stays
RUNNING"), so `_pod_is_runpod_runtime_wedged` returns False → the no-port path
clears the clock + returns `result` unchanged (status stays dead) — fine. But the
plan does not state this interaction or test the both-conditions-true case
(dead + CUDA-IMA tail + transiently no-port).

**Fix:** state the ordering rationale in §4 and add a test for the case where a
CUDA-IMA dead poll coincides with a transient no-port condition, asserting the
CUDA-IMA record is written (not masked by the no-port `running` rewrite). If the
masking is real, the CUDA-IMA escalation may need to run BEFORE the no-port
block, or the no-port `running`-rewrite needs to exempt a CUDA-IMA-signed tail.

mechanizable: yes — a `main()` integration test with a `_PollDouble` returning
`status=dead` + CUDA-IMA `log_tail_excerpt`, plus a `get_pod_by_name` double
returning RUNNING-no-port, asserting the CUDA-IMA record lands.

### MAJOR 3 — Alternatives: a deterministic CODE bug that emits CUDA-IMA twice on the same pod WILL trip the predicate and burn a free-host pivot — the §9 kill-criterion under-weights this

**Grounding.** §9 kill-criterion 1 + §4 dispatch prompt's question ("the FIRST
crash already classified failure_class: code"). The predicate keys on
"same-signature CUDA-IMA twice on the same pod_id." A deterministic code bug
(an indexing error that corrupts a CUDA buffer at a fixed input, a bad custom
kernel) emits IMA every run, reproducibly, on whatever pod it runs on. If the
infra-respawn is in-place same-pod (BLOCKER 1's other branch), two such crashes
on pod-A trip the predicate and pivot to a fresh pod-B — which then ALSO crashes
identically (it's a code bug, not a host wedge), exhausting the once-more bound
and finally parking at `code`/blocked. The plan calls this "bounded once +
benign," which is mostly right (a fresh pod is cheap, the bound holds) — but it
means the predicate cannot distinguish a driver-level host wedge from a
deterministic IMA code bug AT ALL. The only thing separating them is "a fresh
host fixes the wedge but not the bug," and that's discovered by SPENDING the
pivot. This is acceptable for an infra fix (the bound is the safety) but the
plan should be honest that the predicate is "repeat CUDA-IMA," not "host wedge" —
the host-wedge interpretation is a hypothesis the failover TESTS, not a thing the
predicate DETECTS. Note §9 already flags the our-code-frame exclusion as a future
mitigation; making it present-tense for the `failure_classifier`-style
`OUR_CODE_FRAME` check (classifier.py:154) would let a same-signature IMA whose
traceback carries an `src/explore_persona_space/` or `scripts/` frame skip the
pivot. Consider pulling that exclusion forward rather than deferring it.

**Disposition:** not a blocker (the bound makes it benign + bounded), but the §9
framing should be corrected and the our-code-frame exclusion reconsidered for v1
given `OUR_CODE_FRAME` already exists in `failure_classifier.py`.

mechanizable: yes — reuse `failure_classifier.OUR_CODE_FRAME` against the same
wider body surface BLOCKER 2 fixes; a test asserting an IMA-with-our-code-frame
does NOT pivot.

### What's good

The reuse-vs-fork decision (§5) is correct and well-argued: parameterizing
`_relaunch_fresh_runpod` via a `stamp_fn` kwarg (defaulting to the Part C stamp,
byte-unchanged) is the right factoring — forking the inner ~150-line #689-hardened
relaunch would rot. The SEPARATE `runpod_cuda_ima_failover_of` lease field (not
reusing `runpod_wedge_failover_of`) correctly prevents cross-suppression between
a no-port wedge and a CUDA-IMA wedge on the same issue. The two-layer bound
(per-wedge idempotency + per-run once-more) faithfully mirrors the GCP→RunPod
analogue. The decision to NOT fingerprint the exact stack frame (driver IMA has
no stable user-frame) is sound. The `Lease` field add is genuinely additive +
back-compatible (verified against router.py:799-834). Test list is thorough in
breadth (covers first-crash-falls-through, different-pod-id, idempotency,
bounded-once) — the gaps are in the two surfaces above (pod_id reset + excerpt
truncation), which the listed tests assume away rather than exercise.
